# Change (what to research)
Jo's first priority: **"graph engineering"** as a name for what 2.0 is. Jo's own definition (from `PREFERENCES.md` § "Jo's hypothesis of the final shape" — read that section for the verbatim text): nodes = specialised agents/functions; edges = rules and pathways deciding how work flows, including branches and loop-backs for corrections; shared state = the central record that updates and travels with the work.

Establish, from primary sources fetched this session:
1. Whose term it is and where it is used — is "graph engineering" an established name for agent orchestration, a vendor/framework framing, a recent coinage, or several unrelated things sharing the phrase? Search broadly (web_search; include Reddit and practitioner blogs), then fetch the originating pages. Distinguish the phrase from adjacent ones (e.g. "graph-based agent orchestration", "agentic workflows as graphs") and say which the sources actually use.
2. What the practitioners and frameworks that build agent systems as graphs mean by nodes, edges, and shared state — read their own docs/design pages, not summaries. Report the vocabulary each uses and how it lines up with Jo's three parts (table).

# Change (what to research)
Requirements **P-13** (any lane can recall prior work — its own and other lanes', in any repo — *and the decisions made about it*, with provenance, persisting across sessions and the 1.x→2.0 cutover; tool not fixed; ctx is the incumbent) and **P-17** (on resume from compaction or shutdown, a lane's first turn is already grounded in what it was doing — automatic, no re-briefing). Also P-15 (portable machinery; state need not be portable) and P-7a (orchestrator holds lane state).

Candidates to evaluate from primary sources:
1. **ctx** (the incumbent). What it is and what it indexes is partly established first-party: read `/Users/jowolff/code/agent-system-2.0/REVIEW.md` section `## 8. ctx — role versus machinery` and the "ctx corpus" row of § 7 (parent's CLAIMs; cite as such). Add from ctx's own public docs/repo (search for it; the local skill file `/Users/jowolff/.claude/skills/ctx/SKILL.md` names it) what providers/roots it can index, whether OMP/Pi session logs are supported, and whether it stores decisions or only transcripts.

# Change (what to research)
Jo's second priority: **Addy Osmani** on running many coding agents, and specifically the idea Jo calls **"owning the outer loop"**. Plumb does not know what Osmani means by that phrase; do not paraphrase it from memory.

1. Find Osmani's own text for "outer loop" / "owning the outer loop" (his blog addyosmani.com, his newsletter/Substack, his books' public pages, talks with transcripts, his GitHub repos including https://github.com/addyosmani/agent-skills if it carries the idea). Quote the passages that define it. If he uses the phrase differently in different places, show each.
2. Then his other writing on orchestrating multiple agents, agent skills, and the human's role — fetch and cite; cap at what he actually wrote.
3. Extract what he prescribes that bears on: the human's single surface (P-6/P-7), lanes/workstreams (P-2/P-5), verification per step (P-4), planning before execution (P-12), memory (P-13), spend (P-9/P-14), self-improvement (P-16). Table per requirement.
4. Note explicitly anything he assumes that Jo has ruled out (e.g. fleet-scale subscriptions, P-14).

# Change (what to research)

Jo asked, verbatim (PREFERENCES.md P-12): *"i want to know the best way to do it (which will require research - is it omp's own plan mode? is it a skill in agent-superpowers (https://github.com/obra/superpowers) or addy osmani's agent skills https://github.com/addyosmani/agent-skills"*.

Report: what each produces (artifact, format), how the human is gated (approval points), whether planning is separated from execution, how it handles "is this task big enough to plan", and how plans are handed to executing agents/subagents.
2. **addyosmani/agent-skills** (https://github.com/addyosmani/agent-skills) — same questions for its planning/spec-related skills.

# Change (what to research)
Jo's fourth priority, in Jo's words (from `briefs/research.md` item 4): a survey on the open internet of **best-in-class examples of what we're doing** — orchestrators and graph-engineered multi-agent coding systems that people actually run — not limited to named authors. Jo explicitly wants Reddit included for first-hand accounts.

1. Find up to ten candidates across three kinds: (a) frameworks/products for orchestrating multiple coding agents with persistent workers and a single human surface; (b) open-source personal orchestrators individuals have built and written up; (c) first-hand practitioner accounts (blogs, Reddit posts with substance, talks with transcripts) of running several long-lived agents on real work. Prefer sources with a repo or a detailed write-up over announcements.
2. For each: what it is, who runs it, one-paragraph shape (how the human interacts, how work is routed, what persists, how agents spawn sub-agents, how spend/model choice is handled), with CITE receipts from its own docs/repo/post.

Your job is to separate what transfers from what does not.

1. Fetch Yegge's own writing (his Medium/Substack posts, talks with transcripts, GitHub repos, interviews where he speaks first-person) on multi-agent coding, "software factories", agent fleets, orchestration, and the human's role. Cite passages.
2. For each pattern or practice he describes, classify with a receipt: (a) **transfers** — does not depend on many parallel paid subscriptions or fleet scale; (b) **out of means** — depends on it; (c) **unclear** — say what would settle it. Table.

# Lens: what the persona-less, workload-bound lane silently breaks
On 2026-09-23 P-5 was ruled: named persistent lanes are not a tier; persistence is a property of the workload; address = workload name; charter → per-workload brief plus per-repo rules loaded on checkout; memory and per-repo expertise → the P-13 store (see PREFERENCES.md § P-5 'Resolved 2026-09-23' and REQUIREMENTS.md line 14). Read every other P-item as if that ruling is final and find what it silently breaks or leaves undefined: who or what a message is addressed to in P-7c when there is no persona; what 'a lane's ceiling' (P-9, P-7b) attaches to when lanes are born and die with workloads; what P-6 'open any lane directly' means for a lane that does not exist yet; how P-17 resume works for a lane that was closed rather than compacted; how P-3 'cutover one lane at a time' maps 1.x seats (per-repo, named) onto 2.0 lanes (per-workload) — which 1.x seat becomes which lane; whether per-repo rules 'loaded on checkout' collide with P-10/P-11 (every rule re-decided, mechanical where possible); whether anything in P-2's 'his lanes are our marches' still holds. Write the report to /Users/jowolff/agent-scratch/agent-system-2.0/triple-check/abolished-seat.md.

Also flag any P-item whose 'change' column names a Phase 5 dependency that another P-item has already ruled. Write the report to /Users/jowolff/agent-scratch/agent-system-2.0/triple-check/contradictions.md.

# Changes (locate by heading; line numbers are approximate)

6. Interrupt a transition mid-way (kill the process between two writes, or simulate) and show the state afterwards.
7. Competing lane claim: two processes try to claim the same open workload at the same moment. Show which wins and what the loser sees.
